introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

La composante demandée en (iv) est celle de la réaction perpendiculaire à AO ; le corrigé donne sa grandeur et son sens.

questions.enonce_markdown: Show, by integration, that the moment of inertia of a thin uniform circular disc of mass $2m$ and radius $a$ about an axis through the centre, $O$, of the disc and perpendicular to the plane of the disc is $ma^2$. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The disc has area $\pi a^2$ and mass $2m$, so its mass per unit area is $\sigma = \dfrac{2m}{\pi a^2}$.

Divide the disc into thin concentric rings of radius $r$ and width $dr$. The area of a ring is $2\pi r\,dr$, so its mass is

$$dM = \sigma\cdot 2\pi r\,dr = \frac{4m\,r}{a^2}\,dr,$$

and every particle of the ring is at distance $r$ from the axis, so the ring has moment of inertia $r^2\,dM$. Summing over all rings:

$$I_O = \int_0^a r^2\cdot\frac{4m\,r}{a^2}\,dr = \frac{4m}{a^2}\int_0^a r^3\,dr = \frac{4m}{a^2}\cdot\frac{a^4}{4} = ma^2.$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The disc is free to rotate in a vertical plane about a smooth horizontal axis through a point $A$ on the circumference of the disc. The axis is perpendicular to the plane of the disc. Show that the moment of inertia of the disc about this axis is $3ma^2$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
By the parallel axes theorem, with the new axis parallel to the axis through the centre $O$ and at distance $OA=a$ from it:

$$I_A = I_O + (2m)\,a^2 = ma^2 + 2ma^2 = 3ma^2.$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The disc is released from rest when $AO$ is horizontal. Show that $3a\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}\right)^2 = 4g\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle $AO$ makes with the horizontal through $A$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
When $AO$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal, the centre $O$ has fallen a vertical distance $a\sin\theta$ below its starting level (the level of $A$).

Energy is conserved (smooth axis, so the reaction does no work). The disc starts from rest, so the kinetic energy gained equals the potential energy lost:

$$\tfrac12 I_A\dot\theta^2 = 2mg\,(a\sin\theta) \;\Longrightarrow\; \tfrac12(3ma^2)\dot\theta^2 = 2mga\sin\theta$$

$$3a\left(\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right)^2 = 4g\sin\theta.$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the component of the reaction at the axis perpendicular to $AO$ when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate the result of part (iii) with respect to $t$:

$$6a\,\dot\theta\,\ddot\theta = 4g\cos\theta\,\dot\theta \;\Longrightarrow\; \ddot\theta = \frac{2g\cos\theta}{3a}.$$

(This is also $I_A\ddot\theta = 2mg\cdot a\cos\theta$, the torque of the weight about $A$.)

The centre of mass $O$ moves on a circle of radius $a$ about $A$, so its acceleration perpendicular to $AO$ (in the direction of increasing $\theta$, the direction of motion of $O$) is $a\ddot\theta = \dfrac{2g\cos\theta}{3}$.

Let $Y$ be the component of the reaction perpendicular to $AO$, taken in the direction of motion of $O$. The component of the weight $2mg$ in that direction is $2mg\cos\theta$. Newton's second law for the disc (mass $2m$) in that direction:

$$2mg\cos\theta + Y = 2m\cdot\frac{2g\cos\theta}{3}$$

$$Y = \frac{4mg\cos\theta}{3} - 2mg\cos\theta = -\frac{2mg\cos\theta}{3}.$$

When $\theta = \dfrac\pi4$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$:

$$Y = -\frac{2mg}{3\sqrt2} = -\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\,mg.$$

The component of the reaction perpendicular to $AO$ has magnitude $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\,mg\ (\approx 0.471\,mg)$, and the minus sign shows it acts opposite to the direction of motion of $O$ (that is, it has an upward sense).
